#351. 2023 March Madness: Will UConn or San Diego State triumph in the national championship game that 'means everything?'

The University of Connecticut won its fifth men’s basketball national title with a 76-59 victory over San Diego State University on Monday night at NRG Stadium in Houston.

Senior guard Tristen Newton led UConn (31-8) with 19 points and 10 rebounds while Final Four Most Outstanding Player Adama Sanogo, a junior forward, chipped in with 17 points and 10 rebounds.

“We weren’t ranked going into the year so we had the chip on our shoulder,” UConn head coach Dan Hurley told game broadcaster CBS. “We knew the level that we could play at, even through those dark times,” he added, referencing the team’s six losses in eight games during the regular season.

He said going into the tournament his group had confidence garnered during the season.

“And when you have the type of leaders like Andre Jackson (game-high six assists Monday) and Adama Sanogo, they kept this team together, got us back on track and we knew we were the best team in the tournament going in and we just had to play to our level,” he added.

San Diego State (32-7) was topped by Keshad Johnson who had 14 points.

UConn trailed very early but San Diego State was undone by an 11-minute, eight-second stretch in which they scored just five free throws and missed 12 consecutive shots from the field. The Huskies went from down 10-6 to up 36-24 at halftime.

The Aztecs made a run midway through the second half and narrowed the deficit to five at 60-55 with 5:19 to play but the Huskies scored the next nine to take a comfortable lead into the final two minutes.

“We battled. Battled back to five in the second half, but gave them too much separation,” San Diego State coach Brian Dutcher said. “We had to be at our best. We weren’t at our best. A lot had to do with UConn.”

Senior guard Adam Seiko told reporters they gave themselves a chance with their second half comeback but UConn “just made a little bit more plays” at the end.

“They have a lot of weapons. They were pretty good,” said Matt Bradley, also a senior guard. “To beat them, we had to make shots. I shot poorly. And you had to have a really good game to beat those dudes on the offensive end.”

UConn won each of its six tournament games by at least 10 points, with its closest game being a 13-point win over the University of Miami in the national semifinals.

“I just want to thank my teammates, my coaches who believed in me. If it were not for them I would not be here right now,” Sanogo told CBS.

Jordan Hawkins, who scored 16 points for UConn, talked about winning the crown one day after his cousin, Angel Reese of Louisiana State University, won the women’s title.

“I mean it’s absolutely amazing that we both get this opportunity and I mean the family reunion is going to be great so that’s all I know,” he said.

UConn enters rarefied air as only the sixth team to win five NCAA men’s basketball championships, joining UCLA (11), Kentucky (eight), North Carolina (six), Duke (five) and Indiana (five). All of UConn’s titles have come since 1999 with the most recent before Monday occurring in 2014.

UConn’s women’s teams have won 11 basketball national titles.

CNN’s Steve Almasy and Issy Ronald contributed to this report.

#350. A New UK Porn Ban Sparks Fears of Unprecedented Sex Censorship

A new UK law banning porn featuring choking and “fauxcest,” or simulated incest, may have unintended consequences for content creators and smut fans all over the world, some experts warn.

As of November 6, amendments to the Crime and Policing Act will outlaw the “possession or publication of pornographic images of strangulation or suffocation”—a law intended to curb violence against women and girls. Yet some experts warn that the legislation is written broadly enough that it could potentially criminalize far more innocuous content, including “breast smothering,” “jeans facesitting,” and even potentially oral sex, ostensibly because people could have their airways impeded during these activities.

“I would encourage both content creators and consumers to underscore the risks of this law,” says Myles Jackman, an obscenity lawyer in the UK. “Because to me, it genuinely seems like one of the greatest acts of suppression of free speech in global history.”

The new amendments were inspired by a lengthy pornography review authored by Baroness Gabby Bertin, a Conservative member of the UK House of Lords. The legislation bans various depictions of sex acts, including “pornographic images of strangulation or suffocation,” as well as content showing performers role-playing as minors under the age of 16.

It also takes aim at “fauxcest,” an extremely popular porn niche that depicts simulated sexual relations between family members who are not related by blood, such as stepsiblings or stepparents. In Bertin’s review recommending the ban on such content, she cites “anecdotal evidence” suggesting that fauxcest “can be used between an abuser and child to permit interfamily child sex abuse,” describing it as a “fig-leaf” of sorts for actual sexual abuse.

Under the new law, those caught distributing or in possession of such content face up to five years in prison and a fine.

The impending UK legislation has prompted panic among some adult creators, many of whom are currently combing through their content libraries and removing clips that could get swept up in the ban.

“The problem is always how broad [the legislation] is,” says Alexandra Snow, an adult content creator and educator. “And we won't know how they're going to interpret it until they start making people's lives hell.”

Snow says she is particularly concerned about how the aspect of the legislation pertaining to “suffocation or strangulation” will affect kink creators, who may make content related to collaring or leather fetishes. She’s also worried about AI image-recognition software, which is already in widespread use among the platforms, potentially flagging content that isn’t violative at all. “They use a very broad, heavy-handed approach,” she says.

Cami Strella, an OnlyFans creator in the US who estimates that 60 to 70 percent of her content depicts some form of role-play, including step-“fauxcest,” is also concerned about the legislation. She says that the content she makes is “just playing a fantasy,” and that more sex education and literacy is required to teach people about the risks of various behaviors.

“I don’t think banning it is going to do anything,” she says. “If anything, it’ll just push even worse content that is actually illegal or immoral underground, so you’ll have to access it away from these platforms. This is just a slippery slope we’re getting into.”

The new UK law is seemingly targeted at the trend of choking in porn, which has been linked to real-life instances of fatal choking during sex. Though the practice is highly risky, potentially leading to brain damage or death, it’s increasingly common among young adults, largely due to the prevalence of eroticized choking depictions in the media and in porn. The death of a 16-year-old Australian girl in August, who authorities say lost consciousness after she was choked consensually during sex, has led to renewed calls for legislation banning depictions of the practice in online porn, which has “absolutely sort of normalized this kind of sexual violence,” Bertin recently told the BBC.

The UK has a history of imposing stringent restrictions on internet pornography, particularly compared to the United States, where statutes like Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996 largely exempt platforms from liability for hosting objectionable content. Long before many US states started requiring users to verify their ages before visiting porn sites, for instance, the UK communications regulation agency Ofcom has been slapping websites with fines of up to 10 percent of their worldwide revenue for failing to comply with age-verification requirements.

“The UK is really pushing for limits on free speech,” says Michael Fattorosi, an adult industry attorney based in Italy. “This is just something they're throwing on top of the heap of restrictions.”

In a statement to WIRED, Clara Coleman, a spokesperson for the UK’s Ministry of Justice, denied that the legislation was intended to curb sexual expression. “We’re committed to halving violence against women and girls in a decade, and that includes preventing harm before it starts,” Coleman says. “[These] laws aren’t about policing people’s sexual freedom, they’re about cracking down on content that normalizes violence against women, encourages unlawful behavior, and can cause real-world harm.”

Jackman, the lawyer, says that he has no issue with the provision banning strangulation, as its risks are proven and there are existing laws banning strangulation in the UK. He cautions, however, that the law is written broadly enough that relatively innocuous content could also potentially be penalized.

“It would be up to a court to decide this on a case-by-case basis, but given that it would appear that face-sitting by a vagina owner is now arguably suffocation, the insertion of a penis could equally be considered suffocation because it blocks the airways,” he says. In other words, “the UK could have just banned blow jobs” in online pornography.

Though the law currently applies only to consumers and creators in the United Kingdom, the stiff penalties for “possession” of such images—which the law defines as an image being stored on a phone, a hard drive, or in cloud storage—is of particular concern to Fattorosi.

“As far as creators are concerned, if you visit the UK, if you’re going there on holiday, if you’re going there for a conference, you should probably be careful about what you keep on your phone,” he says.

The subscription-based platform OnlyFans is particularly vulnerable, he adds. Though most American porn companies don’t have a substantial presence in the UK, making it difficult for Ofcom to go after them, that doesn’t apply to OnlyFans. The subscription-based platform’s parent company, Fenix International Limited, is based in the United Kingdom and has already faced steep fines from the agency for failure to adhere to age-disclosure requirements.

“If I were OnlyFans,” Fattorosi says, “I’d be very worried about this.” (In a statement, OnlyFans tells WIRED the platform “complies with applicable laws and regulations in all jurisdictions in which it operates and has longstanding, proactive safety measures in place that meet UK legal requirements.”)

In advance of the new legislation taking effect, adult content platforms have issued updated guidelines for creators. The platform IWantClips has already started complying, publishing a new set of guidelines for creators and fans based in the UK and removing clips that could potentially be swept up in the legislation. The laundry list of sexual niches and categories banned now includes “breast smothering,” “ass smothering,” “jeans facesitting,” “BBW facesitting,” “plastic fetish,” “scissorhold,” and “butt drops.”

Trans Princess Jezebel, a dominatrix and adult content creator in the UK, says she has already started going through her content library on IWantClips and OnlyFans, removing videos that may be seen as violative. She’s heavily reliant on clips to advertise her services as a dominatrix, and she’s concerned that once the law takes effect on November 6, she’ll take a huge financial hit.

“When the state starts regulating which types of pornography people are allowed to watch, a dangerous precedent is set,” she tells WIRED in an email. “Where will it end?”

But even though the UK is, for the time being, an outlier, Jackman warns it may not be for long. He says he has heard of lawmakers in Italy, the Netherlands, and Spain discussing similar legislation, as well as members of the evangelical lobby in the United States.

“In terms of free speech,” he says, “the lights are going out across the globe.”

#349. From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs, and why the connection is complicated

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes.

But as Americans vote in the US midterm elections, it's time to think about how disgust shapes our politics, or whether our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.

"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.

But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:

One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.

"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

Indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe."

Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.

"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.

Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.

A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.

However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.

Some early studies suggested conservatives showed stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.

Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.

"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.

Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.

"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it."

The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility."

They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.

But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.

What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

"People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.

Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.

He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.

Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.

"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.

The new study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.

Inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best."

Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.

"I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.

Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.

The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.

"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.

Inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.

"It's one of the many influences on people's politics."

Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.

He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.

"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said. Edited by: Rosalie Delaney

#348. The 10 best hookup apps of 2026: I swiped until my thumb hurt

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

In the age of on-demand everything, it’s no surprise that we can get "dates" (and I use that term loosely) with the tap of a button. Thanks to classic hookup apps like Tinder and newcomers like Pure, finding a sexy new friend can be as straightforward as ordering a pizza. As for the quality? That’s about the same as your pizza — hit or miss, depending on the time of day, where you're located, and how hungry you are.

Fortunately, you’ve got your resident dating app expert here (though I prefer modern-day Carrie Bradshaw) to guide you to the promised land, aka the best hookup apps.

I’ve spent the past four years (yes, years) testing dozens of the top dating apps for Mashable, from discreet sexting apps to dating sites for serious relationships. My goal is simple: to find the best apps for every kind of dater, including the one-night-stand crowd. I also consulted a panel of sex and relationship experts to make sure my picks are solid. The best hookup apps, reviewed by our experts AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections Tinder — top pick for fast hookups Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups Pure — best for anonymous hookups OkCupid — best app for inclusivity

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups

Pure — best for anonymous hookups

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity

The short answer: Tinder is still the best hookup app for most people, thanks to its massive user base and new IRL features like Group Hangouts and Events. If you want total anonymity, try Pure. Hinge is best for regular FWBs, and Feeld is the go-to for kink, ethical non-monogamy, and exploring your sexuality. Queer men should start with Grindr (or Sniffies for cruising), and queer women should download HER.

My first rule: be brutally honest about what you want. Are you here for a good time? Own it. That means staying in your lane; don't go looking for a one-night stand on an app like eharmony. "Hookup apps help prevent situations where people are on mainstream dating sites with the intention of having a casual hookup but are unclear about these intentions," Suzannah Weiss, sex/couples therapist and resident sexologist for Erojoy, tells Mashable. "They also give women a space to be openly sexual creatures without judgment."

And here's a little secret I picked up from Alexander Liebisch, the CEO and founder of TinderProfile.ai: Timing is everything. He found that people messaging on Tinder's "Free Tonight" feature after 10 p.m. on a weekend had a 45 percent higher chance of hooking up.

Once you've matched, reach out, be honest, and follow through! "Plan dates within the first conversation or else you'll get tired out from having a bunch of conversations that aren't going anywhere," Weiss says.

Even after all my testing, if someone asks for the quickest, no-fuss way to find a hookup, my answer is still Tinder. CEO Spencer Rascoff is actively trying to move the app away from its "hookup reputation" to attract Gen Z and bring in more women, but there's likely only one reason you're here.

The irony? His strategy is helping horny singles get laid. New user registrations returned to year-over-year growth in March 2026, per Match Group's latest financials, and daily active users were down just 1 percent in August, Tinder's best showing in years. With over 100 billion connections made worldwide, hookups aren't hard to come by. (Pro tip: Use the "Free Tonight" feature, especially on weekends.)

It's built for rapid-fire connections, not lengthy love stories (though some people, including Mashable's Tech Editor, met their long-term partner on the app).

"Tinder, hands down, is the best app for hookups," Michelle Herzog, LMFT and AASECT-certified sex therapist, tells Mashable. "Over the past decade or so, it’s morphed from being the early 20s hookup central to a place for adults of all ages to go for a quick one-nighter." Weiss adds that it's "probably the most popular hookup app among college students."

Even when Tinder plays dress-up as a serious relationship platform (see: turning "Double Date" into "Modes" and launching the reality show Double Date Island), it's still the undisputed heavyweight champion of casual flings. You can use "Double Date" for low-pressure group hangouts, and Tinder's "Year in Swipe" data crowned 2026 the year of "Clear-Coding," aka laying your intentions on the table so nobody wastes their time.

The newest way to take the pressure off? Group Hangouts, which launched Sept. 30. You and at least two friends pick an activity and "like" other groups. If at least one person from each side likes the other, everyone lands in a shared chat to make plans. This feature is a nice piggyback to its relatively new "Events" tab, which lets you RSVP to low-stakes hangouts like bar trivia or Chinatown mahjong. Tinder plans to expand "Events" to 75 cities by the end of 2026, and about 30 percent of events are free. Tinder is also testing an AI-powered "Missed Connections" feature in Canada and Australia that serves up a weekly list of profiles you've physically crossed paths with.

Of course, there are some AI-related upgrades, too, including a "Chemistry" matchmaker and a revamped algorithm that prioritizes "Sparks," aka real back-and-forth conversations. Just don't let the algorithm do all the thinking for you. "Algorithmic curation, at its current level of sophistication, is very good at showing you more of what you've already responded to and significantly less good at showing you what could work better," says Caroline Millet, a dating burnout coach and former matchmaker. "If your 'type' is so good, why are you still looking?"

Tinder is also cleaning up the grid. In October 2025, it started requiring new members to scan their face (Face Check) to join the app, starting in California, and has expanded the requirement ever since. Scammers found workarounds, but Match Group says Face Check and its other safety updates have cut exposure to potential bad actors by more than 60 percent, and it invests $125 million a year in trust and safety. (Pro tip: If your match gets weird about their photos and tries to immediately move the chat to WhatsApp, unmatch and run.)

Read our full review of AdultFriendFinder.

Pure is for the adventurous dater (and specifically Gen Z, its fastest-growing demographic) who is so over the mainstream options and the endless stream of low-effort "heys." If you want an uncomplicated, no-strings-attached hookup where you can be direct about your desires without judgment, this is the app. It's unconventional, artsy, and built for anonymity. In my experience, it's also the exact place to be for steamy conversations or super-hot phone sex with a stranger. Plus, the app maintains a surprisingly balanced 60/40 male-to-female ratio.

I picked Pure because it's "hot, weird, and way better than Bumble" for making casual connections. Its best features are designed for direct, exciting encounters: chats and photos self-destruct in 24 hours, and the app never even asks for your name, making it a more discreet alternative to mainstream dating apps.

In my four weeks of testing this anonymous hookup app, I was honestly surprised by the results. The conversations were leagues above what I've found on other apps, and I received hundreds of likes daily, even outside of a major city like New York. While anonymity can be a concern, Pure balances it with safety features like Photo Verification and a "True Photo" request, which lets you ask for a live photo in your chat to confirm you're talking to a real person.

To combat the "app fatigue," Pure recently rolled out a major feed redesign in April. You'll now see one profile at a time, making the experience feel much more intentional. The company also added new "Profile Aesthetics" so you can customize your ad with loud color patterns (like bright pink or periwinkle). Bonus: Your "Turn-ons" are now front and center, and a new "Mutual Turn-Ons" view instantly highlights the kinks and interests you share with a potential match before you even say hello.

Pure is also getting serious about safety. In December 2025, the app launched "Safety Signal," a feature that lets you share your live location and date details with a trusted contact when you take things offline. In August 2026, Pure added "My Media Rules," a digital bouncer that lets you set universal boundaries to auto-block all incoming nudes, shut down media sharing completely, or adjust photo permissions on a chat-by-chat basis. It also rolled out AI-powered Age Verification (starting in the UK) to check whether users are adults, and recently partnered with TBD Health to offer at-home STD testing directly through the platform.

"Consent should not begin when two people meet in person. It begins with how someone communicates, what they send and whether they respect a boundary the first time," says Sandra Hatton, a professional matchmaker and founder of When We First. "Technology can create another layer of protection, but it should support consent, not replace the responsibility of users to behave respectfully."

That said, it's a space to navigate with intention. Anonymity is the whole point of Pure, but it shouldn't mean flying blind. "Anonymous should never mean untraceable to YOU," says Erica Arrechea, founder and CEO of Cinqe Matchmaking. "Before meeting someone, know who you're actually meeting. Meet publicly first!"

Weiss also notes that Pure isn't as specifically geared toward the kink and queer communities as Feeld, so you may encounter more straight cis men who are just looking for a conquest. The biggest trade-off is its smaller user base compared to mainstream apps like Tinder, though its recent 95 percent year-over-year registration growth and new status as a top-8 grossing lifestyle app in the U.S., UK, and France show it's rapidly closing the gap.

Don't let Hinge's "designed to be deleted" tagline fool you. In my opinion, it's surprisingly effective for finding regular hookups, especially if you prefer a bit more connection before getting down to business. If you're in a reasonably populated area and want to find people who are a little more intentional, Hinge is a great middle ground when Tinder feels too chaotic.

The catch? Plenty of people are here for a relationship, so please be upfront about wanting something casual. I like it best for finding a regular FWB, not necessarily someone to come over tonight.

Hinge's "Dating Intentions" section lets you state exactly what you're looking for, and according to the app, 75 percent of Gen Z daters check this before sending a "like." Being upfront about wanting something short-term saves everyone time.

Unlike many apps, Hinge lets free users see everyone who "likes" them (one by one), which is a huge plus since most competitors blur out photos until you pay. You get eight free "likes" per day and can chat with matches without paying. Hinge also curates a list of "Standouts" (profiles the algorithm flags as your best potential matches), but you'll need a "Rose" to like them, and you only get one free Rose per week.

To get you offline, "Date Ideas" lets you feature three options on your profile, like grabbing drinks or seeing live music. Potential matches can pick an idea and a time before sending a "like," which beats another vague "we should hang out sometime."

Hinge also launched its "Signals" badge in June. The purple heart highlights verified users with a recent track record of "Thoughtful Participation," like messaging matches and confirming dates. It's a useful clue, not a promise that someone won't flake. "Treat app features as additional information, not proof of intention," says Hatton. "A badge or longer response window can be helpful, but seriousness ultimately shows up through behavior."

If writing your profile or opening a conversation feels overwhelming, Hinge's AI tools can help. "Prompt Feedback" offers nudges to better express your personality, while "Convo Starters" suggests ways to break the ice. Just leave your photos alone; Hinge says 88 percent of its daters are uncomfortable with AI-generated profile pictures.

For added social proof, July's "Friend's Take" feature update lets friends add text, photos, or voice notes to your profile. My advice? Have someone hype up your fun, spontaneous side rather than how "loyal" you are if you're here for casual dating.

On the safety front, Hinge began testing "Face Check" facial verification across key markets earlier this year. It also announced a new approach to minor harassment violations on Oct. 1: Human moderators can issue a warning and require an educational walkthrough before someone can use the app again. Serious or repeated violations can still lead to a ban.

Bumble is the best hookup app for women and non-binary people looking for a casual fling while keeping conversations controlled and low-pressure. In August, Bumble officially ended its famous "women message first" rule, but it still offers a far more structured environment than Tinder: anyone can send just one opening message, and the chat stays locked until the recipient decides to reply.

"Bumble is a helpful app for women who want to avoid being creeped on and only hear from men they're interested in," Weiss tells Mashable. It's also great if you want to find someone who's upfront about wanting "fun, casual dates" or "intimacy, without commitment."

If you're tired of unsolicited messages, Bumble still puts you in the driver's seat, even as the app goes through its biggest shake-up since its 2014 debut. As of August, anyone in a match can send a single opening message, and the chat won't unlock until the recipient replies. To take the pressure off quick-fire texting, Bumble also extended the response window from 24 hours to 72 hours. The change came straight from user feedback: a Bumble survey found that 66 percent of women actually prefer men to send the first message.

Men, this is your moment, so don't waste it on "hey girl." "Read her profile and talk to her like a human being," says Arrechea. "Not 'hey.' Not a copy-and-pasted pickup line." Even on a hookup-friendly app, lead with something from her profile, not your best pickup line.

This update fully replaces Bumble's previous "Opening Moves" feature. And about those rumors that Bumble's AI assistant, "Bee," would replace swiping? CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd shut that down on the company's latest earnings call: "Let me be clear: Bee is not replacing the swipe. We are not aiming for an AI-driven experience. Bee is simply the intelligence under the hood," she said. She's keeping whatever does replace the swipe under wraps for now, with bigger profile and IRL updates expected in early 2027. In the meantime, Bumble added profile badges for "ethical non-monogamy" and "intimacy without commitment," making it easier to flag exactly what you want.

Once your profile is set, Bumble is testing new ways to help you meet up IRL. They're currently testing a "Suggest a Date" feature in Canada to bypass the tedious back-and-forth. (And don't worry about losing your agency; in Canadian tests of these recent changes, 92 percent of women said they still felt in control of their dating experience.)

If you're burned out on one-on-one setups, the app is also launching a standalone event-curation app called "Plans" to help singles meet up in curated small groups in person. You can also use the "Instant Match" QR code to vet your real-life crushes at a bar and check their verified status before you decide to go home with them.

However, it's worth being upfront about the app's fumbles. A class-action lawsuit alleges that Bumble failed to protect user data during a "massive" breach by the hacker group ShinyHunters earlier this year. Reuters reported in late June that Bumble is exploring a potential sale, and its paying user base has dropped to 3.2 million, down 24 percent from two years ago. Even Blackstone, one of its biggest investors, is cashing out.

Despite the drama and a challenging market, Bumble still offers solid functionality. You can chat via text, voice, or video without spending a dime, and free users still have access to basic filters like age, distance, and verified profiles. While premium features (Bumble Boost or premium membership) offer advanced filters, they're not essential for finding a potential hookup buddy.

Feeld is for the explorers: the singles, couples, and polycules looking to ethically explore non-monogamy, kink, and alternative relationship styles. If you find the binary options on most dating apps to be limiting, Feeld's inclusive, consent-forward environment is refreshing. It’s a hub for people practicing "relationship anarchy" or just curious about connections without traditional rules.

It's worth noting, however, that the app is attracting more "vanilla" users (those with conventional tastes) lately, which is changing the dynamic somewhat. But even those "normies" might be hiding a wild side: Feeld's "State of Reflections Volume 1: Am I Normal?" report found that 42 percent of mainstream, non-Feeld daters actually practice kink. And the community is getting more curious by the day.

"Heteroflexible" is the fastest-growing sexuality on the app, and interest in pegging among cis men has surged. It's proof that this is still the place to go if you want to explore outside the box. And yes, the nerds are here. New Feeld data found that tabletop gamers are 65 percent more likely to be non-monogamous than other users, and more than half of Gen Z Feeld members list ethical non-monogamy as an interest.

Feeld joins Hinge and Hily on the very short list of dating apps that are gaining new users, even as other apps struggle.

The free “Constellation” feature lets you be transparent by linking your profile with up to five partners, and you can use more than 20 labels to define those connections, from "Lover" and "Dom" to "Friend with benefits." (While this feature links your profiles, your private chat histories and existing connections are not shared with your partners.) The app also offers detailed desire and kink tags, from "Bondage" to "Cuddling," so you can find exactly what you're looking for.

"Feeld is a good app for finding hookups because the people on it are sexually open-minded but also conscious," says Weiss. "Many of them are looking for casual sexual encounters, but not 'casual' in the sense of wanting to make a conquest or put in minimal effort," she adds. "I often recommend this app to couples who want to find a third person to play with or date, as well as singles who want to explore different sexual fantasies and subcultures."

To make articulating those desires even easier, Feeld launched an interactive quiz called "Reflections" that helps you map out your boundaries, relationships, and kink affinities. According to Feeld's May 2026 "State of Reflections Volume 2: The Words We Didn’t Have" report, it's super effective for skipping the small talk and getting down to business. After taking the quiz, 72 percent of users said they changed (or thought about changing) how they communicate their desires on their profiles, and over half felt more empowered to bring up boundaries and safe sex right from the start. Once you finish the quiz, you get a custom link and QR code to share your dealbreakers with potential partners before you even meet.

If you're still figuring out how to put your relationship structure into words, Weiss suggests keeping it playful: "You can write something cute like 'ethical slut' or 'I have room for more than one love of my life in my heart' instead of just using the technical language."

If you're tired of Tinder, I think HUD is the best new hookup app, and its tagline is literally "Fun without strings attached." HUD stands for "Honest, Upfront, and Direct," and it's the app for people who aren’t afraid to be their most authentic selves. Translation: If you're into non-monogamy, this is where you'll find like-minded people.

The people on this app aren’t here to find their forever person, but friends with benefits is definitely on the table. You might also find kinksters, ethical non-monogamous folks, and people interested in exploring relationship styles that are a little outside the mainstream. With more than 19 million users worldwide as of 2026, HUD offers many opportunities for your next hookup.

If Hinge and Pure had a baby, it would be HUD. This app doesn’t beat around the bush, but it’s also artsy in presentation and has a kinky-fun community behind it.

Like Hinge, you can answer prompts (up to three), add photos (up to five), and note whether you’re into smoking, drinking, or drugs. There’s also a really cool "My Bedroom" feature that lets you choose three "desires" that you’re really into, three "desires" you’re "open" to, and three you’re definitely not into. Examples include "bondage," "butt stuff," and "golden showers." There are tons of "desires" to choose from, even if you’re not that kinky, so have fun with it.

Speaking of kinky, HUD just published its 2026 Pleasure Census (a global culture report in partnership with Girls Get Off). The survey revealed that 80 percent of daters aren't having as much sex as they'd ideally like, and those who openly talk about what they want in bed are three times more likely to reach orgasm with a partner every time. That's why features like "My Bedroom" are so great; they eliminate that awkward barrier to communication before you even meet up.

In addition to its "My Bedroom" feature, HUD also has an "Anti-Commitment Mode" badge you can add to your profile to let potential matches know why you're here. You’ll also get to pick your archetype (if you’re not sure what yours is, the app has a little quiz) to help you find your match. You can even add your favorite song to your profile.

Not sure how to explain that you're poly, kinky, or just not looking for anything serious? Keep it short. "You don't need to write a manifesto in your dating bio!" says Paulita Pappel, intimacy expert and founder of Lustery. "The bio is there to open the right door, not to function as a legal contract."

The chat features are also a little more developed than those in a typical hookup app. You can engage with someone’s profile just by liking or commenting on their prompts, photos, etc. The video chat option also shows both cameras blurred until you both decide to reveal yourselves. Of course, you can get more features with a premium subscription, but the free version offers a lot.

Hily (short for "Hey, I Like You") is for anyone who wants a little more substance than Tinder's fast-swipe format but doesn't want to answer a ton of questions to get set up and start matching. This new dating app gives you total flexibility: you can keep your profile simple, or fill out optional prompts, pick lifestyle passions, and take its 40-question "Icks&Clicks" compatibility quiz to see how compatible you are with potential matches before chatting.

Granted, my experience comes from living in a small Southern town (where more than 1,400 men were active at any given moment), but even compared to testing Hinge in the same spot, Hily brought out a distinct crowd. The user pool was packed with blue-collar guys, hunters, fishers, and dudes on motorcycles looking for low-pressure hangouts, casual flings, or sexting partners. While I didn't run into many queer women (mostly couples looking for a third), if you're looking for straight hookups with outdoorsy or country-leaning guys, the active user base makes finding a match easy.

Read our full review of the Hily dating app.

Even though it doesn't get as much attention as Tinder or Bumble, Hily has over 42 million users and lets you control how much effort you put into your profile. You can pick intentions like "Physical connection" or "Something casual," list up to 12 passions, and answer optional prompts under categories like "My Dating Guide" and "Life Vibes." It also features a "Roulette" wheel that hands out free daily perks like profile boosts and rollbacks.

There are a couple of quirks to keep in mind while browsing, though. While the "Finder" will show you people who match your set filters (like age, location, and gender), those preferences don't necessarily apply to who lands in your "Likes" feed. Plus, anyone who likes your profile stays blurred unless you pay for a subscription — unless you get lucky and win free "Unblurs" from the daily Roulette wheel or happen to stumble across them naturally in the "Finder."

If you're not too keen on receiving NSFW photos or chats, Hily added a feature called "Consent Guard." Built with sexologists, this tool scans incoming messages and photos for adult content and gives you a pop-up warning so you can decide whether you actually want to see a nude or explicit text before opening it. It keeps your inbox safe from surprise cyberflashing, but lets you turn up the heat as soon as you give the green light. "[Consent tools] make it less likely for users to be sexually harassed, while also allowing them to see who the culprits are so they can choose not to engage with them," says Weiss.

While other apps push AI matchmakers, Hily is taking a different approach. Their early 2026 "T.R.U.T.H. Report" showed that nearly 70 percent of daters feel AI matchmakers make dating feel fake. In response, Hily brought back its "HI" (Human Intelligence) campaign to focus on real human chemistry rather than automated matching algorithms.

Grindr is the hookup app for gay men. While there are other options on the market, Grindr is the go-to spot for most gay, bi, trans, and queer men looking for a fast connection. It's undeniably effective for finding a hookup, and the numbers prove it: Grindr's "Unwrapped" report revealed that users sent over 135 billion chats last year, with "Hung" being the most-searched profile tag.

However, as Tyler Schoeber pointed out in his review, the free tier is "overrun with intrusive ads" and limits you to viewing around 87 messageable profiles on the grid unless you pay for an upgraded subscription. Unfortunately, a Grindr XTRA membership can get pricey fast. Thankfully, Grindr's 2026 roadmap promises to improve the ad experience with "rewarded ads," which will let free users unlock premium features just by watching an ad.

The bottom line: Thanks to its wide user base, Grindr is still the go-to hookup app for gay men, even if the free version can be a pain to use.

Grindr's ability to connect you with nearby guys instantly is unmatched, especially in smaller towns where the queer community might be limited. Its location-based grid makes it incredibly easy to find someone available right now. This year, they're putting the "Right Now" feature directly onto the map so you can see exactly who's ready to hook up nearby. According to Grindr's own data (released in May), this feature is most used in places like Taiwan, the Philippines, Lima, Buenos Aires, and Medellín. They also added "Discreet Posting," which lets you post a hookup request without showing your profile until you manually approve a chat request.

Aside from getting your biscuit buttered, Grindr has become a hub for travelers. In fact, to capitalize on its global footprint, the app just dropped the third season of its Host or Travel series. This jet-setting culture led to the "Roam" feature, which lets you drop a pin anywhere in the world to scout local talent before you even pack your bags. The app's map is also getting a serious upgrade to highlight gay bars, clubs, and gyms, with direct hotel bookings currently in beta testing.

Grindr has also been flexing some serious cultural muscle, most recently teaming up with Madonna to launch her Confessions II album with a surprise Times Square concert streamed exclusively to Grindr users.

The biggest news in 2026 is that Grindr is officially entering its "AI era" — and it might cost you. The app recently started testing its ultra-premium subscription tier called "EDGE." Powered by Grindr's proprietary "gAI" stack, this tier costs $350–$500 a month and is designed to reduce scrolling. Free users aren't entirely left out, though; they'll get AI perks like real-time chat translations, a "Smart Inbox," and an AI "Wingman" to help filter matching profiles.

Last year, the company publicly supported the "App Store Accountability Act," arguing that age verification should happen at the device level (via Apple or Google) rather than forcing users to upload IDs to every app. They also added an in-app Safety Center, a "Taken on Grindr" timestamp to verify photo freshness, and rolled out impressive sexual health features (backed by their Grindr for Equality initiative), including automated HIV testing reminders, status sharing, and PrEP/DoxyPEP profile options.

There's more on the healthcare front, too. In September, Grindr agreed to acquire Freddie's parent company, PurposeMed, with plans to expand access to PrEP care through Grindr Health. The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026.

While the free experience can feel bogged down by ads that push users toward paid tiers like XTRA, Grindr is still the undisputed King for quick, location-based connections in the gay community.

HER is a platform created by and for queer women, providing a safe and inclusive space to connect with women and nonbinary folks without worrying about being sexualized by "skeevy men." Launched in 2015 to meet a growing need in the lesbian dating scene, HER isn't exclusively designed for hookups, but it offers a vibrant community where you can explore casual encounters or even find meaningful relationships. With more than 15 million users, the app is brimming with opportunity for whatever you're looking for.

HER makes it easy to signal your intentions. The "Looking for" section on your profile lets you add a "something casual" tag, which is displayed out in the open. More recently, the app introduced "Feelings," a feature that lets you add temporary, expressive tags to your profile like "Hook up" or "Flirty" to show exactly what kind of connection you're craving.

The app also functions like a social media platform, creating an inclusive space for LGBTQ+ users with a social feed, events, and media. While the interface can feel a little clunky at first, it's not too difficult to navigate. For safety, HER offers photo-verified profiles with a checkmark badge.

In 2025, HER was acquired by Match Group. The move was met with apprehension from its user base, with many on Reddit fearing the "enshittification" of another beloved queer platform. While HER founder Robyn Exton expressed optimism and Match Group CEO Spencer Rascoff pledged to "protect" what makes the app special, the sapphic community is largely holding its breath to see if they live up to that promise. Those fears aren't entirely unfounded; Match Group recently reported a 20 percent revenue increase in HER test markets due to new "monetization optimizations," which have some users wary of future paywalls.

However, the app's core features are pretty much the same. HER even kicked off the year with a new "Sapphic Restart" campaign to reassure users of its community-first approach. If you're wondering if the company still has an edge, look at its "Everything Reminds Me of HER" billboards in New York and Los Angeles. The brazen ads featured highly sensual innuendos — like champagne cascading over skin and fingers slipping into a bowling ball. The campaign went viral on TikTok and Instagram (because, why wouldn't it?), proving that at least for now, HER is keeping its unapologetic, sex-positive spirit alive. We haven't seen any major degradation in the user experience — so for now, it's still a top recommendation.

Sniffies is a web-based cruising platform built for one thing: finding sex, right now, with minimal small talk. Sniffies was deemed too hardcore for the App Store, and so it's not technically an app. It's a hookup destination for men seeking men who want spontaneous and anonymous encounters.

If you feel like Tinder and Grindr aren't direct enough, I'd like to introduce you to Sniffies, the hookup platform that brings cruising into the 21st century. It launched an official iOS app in March 2025, only to be kicked out of the App Store by May for being, well, too horny for Apple. But if you downloaded the app before it was removed, and haven't deleted it, it should still work.

As soon as you enter the website, you'll see a map of guys nearby who are looking for action in your area. (You don't have to deal with registering for an account or anything — pull up the site, choose to browse anonymously, complete the age verification and captcha, and you're in.) The "Cruiser Filters" let you search for exactly what you're into, from body type to endowment size to your favorite sex positions.

As of April 2026, Sniffies is doubling down on speed with a few new updates. They just dropped "Cruiser Cards," a scrollable carousel that highlights active guys nearby so you don’t have to hunt around the map. They’ve also added a new "Into Filter" and "Position Icons" that put a cruiser’s intent and favorite sex positions directly on their map avatar.

When you're ready to meet, you can use the new "Share a Spot" feature to drop a temporary, expiring map pin directly into the chat. It’s much better than sending vague directions or swapping apps to share your location. They even added "Share a Group," which lets you send live group event details — like the time and who’s attending.

The app now has around three million monthly active users who send 20 million messages daily, and has even caught Match Group's attention. The company just invested $100 million in Sniffies, a deal that also gives Match an option to buy the platform outright.

If your idea of a perfect match is someone who can discuss the nuances of rope suspension one minute and step in as Dungeon Master for your next D&D night the next, you should probably be on FetLife. To be clear, FetLife is a social network for the kink community, not a hookup app in the typical sense. That means users might not appreciate it if you treat it like a swiping or swinging app. Still, as the online destination for established kinksters, it's a great place to meet new sexy friends who share your very specific interests.

We also think FetLife is a great place if you're looking for the best hookup app for gamers, for lack of a better option. While there isn't a hookup app made exclusively for gamers (at least, not one worth recommending), FetLife's user base includes a lot of self-described nerds, and there's a surprising amount of overlap between the gaming and kink communities.

Unlike swipe-based apps, FetLife operates as a social network. Weiss also recommends FetLife as a great destination for those with nerdy interests: "FetLife is popular among gamers and even has some subgroups specifically for kinky gamers," says Weiss. "The app/site tends to attract nerds and other fringe communities."

OkCupid (removed October 2026): OkCupid is still a solid pick for inclusive, values-driven dating, but it's a relationship app at heart. Feeld, HUD, and HER all do inclusivity better for no-strings fun. And after OkCupid's 2026 FTC settlement over sharing nearly 3 million users' photos with a facial recognition company, I'm not comfortable recommending it for something as private as hookups.

Hily (added August 2026): I’ve added Hily to our top picks because its free tier is surprisingly generous (up to 100 likes a day!) and its AI safety tech (like Consent Guard) makes it a standout option for casual, blunt daters looking for a fresh alternative to the Big Three.

Hinge (moved up October 2025): Hinge just keeps getting better, so I’ve bumped it up higher on my list. It still earns its spot for casual dating with personality; its user base is growing, and my recent tests have been surprisingly positive.

You might notice a few apps that pop up in ads or other lists are missing here. That’s intentional. I swipe through the good, the bad, and the downright sketchy so you don’t have to. For an app to make my list, it has to be effective, safe, and worth your time.

Here's a shortlist of apps that didn't make the cut:

Plenty of Fish: POF's rebrand didn't do it any favors. My last round of testing showed it removed key features like free messaging with non-matches, and I kept running into the same old profiles. (Removed January 2025.)

Match: Some people swear they've found casual hookups on Match, but that's not what it's for. It's still one of my top picks for a long-term relationship. For a hookup? You're fishing in the wrong pond. (Removed August 2025.)

Wild: You’ve probably seen ads for this one. On paper, Wild sounds like the perfect casual dating app. In practice, the paywalls are aggressive, the distance filter doesn't work, and you have to pay for anything that's even remotely useful. Unless you're willing to spend serious cash upfront (and hope for the best), the experience feels more limited than with more generous free options like Tinder or Hily.

DOWN: This app (formerly "Bang With Friends") is known for its simple "Get Down" vs. "Get Date" feature. It sounds clever, but in reality, the experience is messy at best. Many users report feeling scammed by subscriptions that don't deliver matches, or finding that the few real people on there are... let's say "odd." It’s hard to recommend an app when the main user complaint is "Is anyone real?" Hard pass.

Facebook Dating: Yes, Facebook has a dating section, and it’s surprisingly massive (and completely free, which is huge). While it's a decent option for casual dating, the vibe tends to be a bit more "friends of friends" and "relationship-focused" than the anonymous, no-strings energy you get from apps like Pure or Feeld. (For Mashable's Chance Townsend, signing up was "the most uneventful dating experience" of his life.) It's also added an AI dating assistant and "Meet Cute," which sends you one surprise match a week. It's worth a shot if you're already on Facebook, but it didn't quite crack my top tier for no-strings-attached hookups specifically.

Tinder is the best hookup app for most people because nearly everyone is on it, which means more chances to find someone looking for the same thing. For total anonymity, try Pure. For kink or ethical non-monogamy, go with Feeld. Queer men should start with Grindr or Sniffies, and queer women should try HER.

Yes. Tinder is trying to shake its hookup reputation with features like Events, Modes, and its brand-new Group Hangouts, but it's still the fastest way to find a casual connection. If anything, those IRL features make it even easier to meet someone in person, fast.

Tinder, Hinge, and Hily are the best free options. Tinder has the biggest free user pool, Hinge lets free users see who liked them, and Hily's free tier gives you up to 100 "likes" a day. Some apps, like Grindr, have gotten much more limited without a subscription.

Pure is the best anonymous hookup app. It never asks for your name, and chats and photos self-destruct after 24 hours. Just remember that anonymous doesn't mean you shouldn't be cautious: "Anonymous should never mean untraceable to YOU," says Arrechea. Use Pure's True Photo request to confirm you're talking to a real person before you meet.

Bumble is the best hookup app for women who want control over who reaches out. Only one opening message is allowed, and the chat stays locked until you reply. Pure is also free for women and lets you auto-block unsolicited nudes, and HER is our top pick for queer women.

Feeld is the best app for couples looking for a third. Its free Constellation feature lets you link your profile with up to five partners, so everyone's on the same page. "I often recommend this app to couples who want to find a third person to play with or date," says Weiss.

Yes, as long as you stick to apps with built-in protections and practice common sense when meeting strangers. When choosing which dating apps to use, look for features such as:

Photo or face verification: Tinder's Face Check requires new members to take a video selfie.

Nude filters: Pure's My Media Rules and Hily's Consent Guard block or warn you about explicit photos.

Location sharing: Pure's Safety Signal shares your live location with a trusted friend.

Blocking and reporting: Never use an app that makes it hard to report bad behavior.

Always meet in a public place first, get yourself there and home, and tell a friend where you'll be. "Casual sex does not require casual safety," says Sandra Hatton, professional matchmaker and founder of When We First. "Do not give a stranger your home address simply because the intention of the connection is casual." Weiss also recommends having a friend check in with you later that night or the next morning.

They pressure you to drink or host immediately.

They try to move the chat to WhatsApp right away.

Be honest and specific about what you want, like "Looking for a regular FWB" or your specific kinks if you're on Feeld. You don't need to spell out every detail. "The bio is there to open the right door, not to function as a legal contract," says Pappel.

Yes, Hinge works great for casual dating if you use the "Dating Intentions" section. Put "Short-Term" or "Figuring it out" on your profile so everyone knows why you're there. The profile prompts also help you gauge someone's personality before you meet up.

Go with Tinder if you want volume, since it has the biggest user base by far. Go with Bumble if you want a slower, more controlled pace. Only one opening message is allowed, and the chat doesn't unlock until the other person replies (they have 72 hours).

Yes, Scruff and Sniffies are great alternatives. Grindr still has the most guys online, but Scruff is the best pick for a more rugged, conversational crowd, and Sniffies is the place for map-based cruising.

In some cases, such as if you live in a small town or don't have time to wait for matches. In our Grindr review, we noted that Grindr Xtra can be worthwhile when you're traveling or during big events. However, you can typically make connections on apps like Tinder or Grindr using only the free versions.

Most hookup apps are free to download but lock key features, like seeing who liked you, behind a paywall. Hily and Tinder let you match and chat for free, while apps like Grindr and Feeld save their best features for paying members.

Recommending the best hookup apps isn't something I take lightly. Your time and, more importantly, your safety matter to me. That's why my selection process involves much more than blindly swiping left and right to see who is online.

If you're wondering how we choose the top platforms for casual dating, here’s exactly how I make sure my recommendations are trustworthy and genuinely helpful:

Hands-on testing: I personally create profiles and test out every single platform on this list, whether it's a mainstream app or a mobile hookup site like Sniffies. I look at how matching algorithms work in the real world and prioritize platforms that are intuitive, effective, and offer robust safety features (such as photo verification and reporting tools to prevent catfishing). If an app feels clunky, pushes too many annoying ads, or just gives off a bad vibe, it doesn't make the cut.

Expert and community feedback: I cross-reference my first-hand findings with real user reviews (yes, including Reddit threads) and consult with top relationship experts to ensure my picks are comprehensive. For this guide, I gathered insights from:

Suzannah Weiss, sex/couples therapist and resident sexologist for Erojoy

Sandra Hatton, professional matchmaker and founder of When We First

Erica Arrechea, founder and CEO of Cinqe Matchmaking

Caroline Millet, dating burnout coach and former matchmaker

Paulita Pappel, intimacy expert and founder of Lustery

Alexander Liebisch, CEO and founder of TinderProfile.ai

Michelle Herzog, LMFT, and AASECT-certified sex therapist

Continuous monitoring: The casual dating app world changes fast. My work doesn't stop after I hit publish. I continuously monitor app performance and feature updates, which means I'm ready to make tough calls and update my recommendations anytime an app no longer lives up to its promise.

Tabitha Britt is an award-winning freelance journalist, editor, and SEO/AEO strategist. Aside from reviewing dating apps and sex toys for Mashable, Tabitha is also the founding editor-in-chief of DO YOU ENDO — a digital magazine by individuals with endometriosis, for individuals with endometriosis. She has a Master's degree in Creative Publishing and Critical Journalism from The New School for Social Research and is a grad of Sextech School. You can find more of her work in various online publications, including National Geographic, Glamour, Better Homes & Gardens, and Everyday Health.

#347. NYT demands Brave shut down its paywall blocker and end deals with AI firms

Lawsuit calls Brave “supplier, dealer, and distributor” of stolen news content.

The New York Times and other newspaper companies sued Brave Software yesterday, alleging that the browser maker illegally bypasses paywalls and sells stolen news content to AI companies.

“Brave is the supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content for its own users and many of the most prominent GenAI companies, including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere,” the NYT alleged in a lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Southern District of New York. Citing third-party revenue estimates, the suit claimed that “Brave has made more than $100 million by copying and reselling publishers’ work without consent or permission,” while “publishers have received nothing.”

The lawsuit said, “AI companies pay Brave to provide them with real-time online content from the Brave search index,” and use content from the Brave index “to train their own AI models” and “to respond to specific user queries.” The NYT lawsuit points to Brave’s website, which says the Brave Search API is “used by some of the biggest names in AI, including Cohere, Mistral, Perplexity, and You.com.”

The lawsuit accused Brave of all the major types of copyright infringement: direct infringement, contributory infringement, and vicarious infringement. The lawsuit claims Brave infringes copyrights directly by scraping articles for its search index, for its “Ask Brave” AI search feature, and for the Brave API that “serves as an illicit source of unlicensed copyrighted material, including Times journalism, to other AI companies.”

The NYT accused Brave of being “a contributory and vicarious infringer when it deliberately induces, facilitates, controls, and profits from its users’ and GenAI customers’ copying of the copyrighted content.” Finally, the lawsuit said Brave violated the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) by circumventing technological measures the NYT and other content owners use to restrict access to their articles.

“The Brave Browser includes a default setting that, when activated, causes the browser to go behind website paywalls and provide the paywalled content to the user,” the lawsuit said. The browser “blocks advertising that would otherwise appear on The Times’s website, and instead shows its own ads, offering its users a cut of the revenue even as it deprives The Times of digital advertising revenue that helps it fund the expensive effort of producing journalism,” the lawsuit said.

When testing the Brave browser for Mac today, we found that the optional “paywall blocker” feature made it possible to read a paywalled New York Times article. The feature was enabled in the default settings and can be turned off.

The NYT asked for a permanent injunction to stop Brave from continuing the allegedly illegal conduct. The lawsuit seeks statutory damages, actual damages, restitution of profits derived from alleged copyright infringement, and “restitution and disgorgement of all revenue and profits Brave obtained through its ad-substitution scheme.”

A similar lawsuit was filed against Brave in the same court yesterday by the New York Daily News, Chicago Tribune, and Orlando Sentinel companies. “AI giants are now desperate to avoid getting caught red-handed stealing news from publishers, so Brave Software is selling them a back door to the journalism they know they have no right to,” said Steven Lieberman, a lawyer for the plaintiffs. “Buying stolen goods secondhand doesn’t make them legitimate. Brave must be held responsible for laundering pirated reporting for the AI industry.”

We contacted Brave and will update this article if it provides a response. Perplexity, which is not a defendant in the Brave lawsuit but is facing a different lawsuit filed by the NYT, accused the news organization of “disinformation” in a statement provided to Ars and other news outlets. Perplexity’s statement did not identify any specific inaccuracies in the lawsuit against Brave.

“The New York Times is overpaying its attorneys and underpaying its journalists. (Who could’ve easily identified the disinformation in this suit.),” Perplexity’s statement said.

The NYT sued Perplexity in December 2025, alleging that its AI tool gives users “outputs that are identical or substantially similar to” NYT articles, including “verbatim or near-verbatim reproductions, summaries, or abridgements of the original content.” Perplexity’s response to that lawsuit said its answer engine only fetches content from copyrighted articles in reply to user queries. Perplexity argued that “developing an AI tool that can allegedly automatically fetch and provide specific content in response to user requests based on its pre-configuration and access to materials available on the Internet” is not “volitional conduct.”

The NYT also sued OpenAI and Microsoft in December 2023 in a lawsuit alleging that OpenAI trains its AI with stolen news content. The lawsuit is heading toward a trial, with OpenAI arguing that its use of news articles is fair use under copyright law.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#345. Israel Is Destroying the Machinery South Lebanon Needs to Rebuild

They had bulldozers and excavators, the machines needed to clear the rubble, but they were afraid to use them. Instead, locals began clearing the debris by hand after Israeli strikes hit southern Lebanon throughout 2025. These weren’t just people’s homes; they were also businesses that had construction equipment—the kind that could have made recovering far less arduous—but the machines’ owners feared that bringing them out would invite another attack.

“They felt that just the presence of this heavy machinery that was typically used in reconstruction was a threat,” said Ramzi Kaiss, a Human Rights Watch (HRW) researcher in Lebanon.

Reconstruction depends on more than replacing buildings that have been lost. Roadways need to be cleared, water networks must be restored, and there need to be factories that can supply construction materials and equipment. However, reports from HRW, aid workers, and UN peacekeepers have documented how Israeli attacks have been damaging those systems and how the fear of further strikes has obstructed their repair.

“We did see incidents in which construction equipment was unfortunately targeted, which made it difficult,” said Kandice Ardiel, a spokesperson for the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL). “Not just for these repairs and the removal of rubble to happen, but again, for people to return to their lives.”

Many residents did return after the 2024 fighting, “and they did rebuild,” said Ardiel. But afterward, “we’ve seen things just destroyed again.”

In a December 2025 investigation, HRW examined four Israeli attacks on heavy-machinery showrooms and maintenance facilities as well as a factory that produced cement and asphalt. The strikes took place between August and October 2025, after the November 2024 ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah. Human Rights Watch reported that the attacks destroyed more than 360 pieces of construction equipment and classified the strikes as apparent war crimes.

Each of these targets had large supplies of necessary resources. Kaiss visited four of these sites, across which she saw a massive scale of destruction: “These are hundreds and hundreds of heavy machinery used in reconstruction-related processes.”

The Israeli military said on Telegram that the equipment and materials supported, or were intended to support, Hezbollah’s reconstruction of its infrastructure. HRW said it found no evidence of military targets at or around the sites. Though the organization could not establish the intended use of every attacked machine or store of materials, it did not find any evidence that these supplies were intended for military use. HRW did, however, verify civilian uses for some equipment.

And though reconstruction has stalled, the destruction has continued. By Israeli defense minister Israel Katz’s own count, 23,000 homes and more than 60 villages have been destroyed as of October. A New York Times analysis found that Israeli forces have largely leveled 48 of the roughly 60 villages and towns in the area they occupy, most of them after the renewed ceasefire in April. The Israeli military told the Times it had received no directive to carry out widespread damage to structures or to demolish villages. (WIRED Middle East contacted the Israel Defense Forces for comment but received no response at the time of publication.)

Beyond the buildings themselves, damage to critical infrastructure, such as water sources, has also halted people’s ability to return home. Doctors Without Borders stated in September that attacks on already weakened water systems continued despite the April ceasefire.

During UN consultations, local officials in Jabal Amel reported that around 6,500 displaced families could not return to a dozen villages inside the zone. These were inside the Israeli-declared “Yellow Line,” which marks a military zone in southern Lebanon, and restrictions in this area have obstructed efforts to restore essential services.

Charlene Silvin, a Doctors Without Borders project coordinator, led a team that visited about 20 towns in the Bint Jbeil area to document damage to water supplies. “There was not one village on the road that was not hit in some capacity,” she said.

Silvin created an account tracing damages from water sources to people’s homes. In this region, the boreholes—deep vertical shafts used as wells—that supply the villages with water lie in a valley held by Israeli troops. Not only is access difficult, but many components of the water infrastructure were damaged. There were storage tanks that could no longer hold water, and pump and filtration units were offline. These were supposed to be powered by solar energy, but nearly every panel Silvin and her team surveyed had been damaged.

In the municipality of Yater, Doctors Without Borders installed less ideal plastic tanks, because the main water tank was deemed irreparable. In Froun, the organization took a different approach, repairing the filtration unit and connecting it directly to the water source, bypassing the damaged tank. This is just a small sample of the needed repairs. The group noted in its September 2026 statement that it had documented damage to wells, pumps, generators, filtration units, and pipelines across southern Lebanon.

The attacks on heavy machinery and water resources collide in multiple ways, including the fact that construction vehicles are sometimes necessary to even reach broken pumps. In a 2026 account of repairs, UNIFIL described surveying a 280-meter access route for a maintenance crane. Most of the route was damaged and blocked by berms—mounds of compacted dirt sometimes used as barriers in military conflicts. Peacekeepers had to clear these before they could bring in equipment to repair the well.

Some are relying on trucked-in water, like the 90 families who returned to Zawtar Al-Gharbiyeh, which once had 500 households. This, however, isn’t a long-term solution but an expensive and limited substitute. “It’s not a system,” Silvin said. “It’s a drop.”

The threat of another attack also shapes what gets repaired. “Anyone that would be investing in repairing the infrastructure would be doing so with the fear that the intervention is damaged again in a very short while,” Silvin added.

For her team, that means often opting for temporary fixes rather than the lasting infrastructure residents need. An October UN report also described municipalities struggling to pay staff, fuel pumps, and maintain vehicles, and some local water authorities and civil servants told Silvin that Israeli forces had intimidated them when they tried to reach damaged sites near the Yellow Line.

Approximately 330,000 people remain internally displaced in Lebanon, according to UN estimates as of September 29. But documenting the obstructions people in this region face will also soon change. UNIFIL, which monitors and reports violations in southern Lebanon, is approaching the end of its mandate on 31 December 2026. In an October statement, the organization said discussions were continuing over the UN’s role after this deadline passes.

Ardiel describes the peacekeepers as “the impartial record keepers of what’s happening on the ground.” Their departure raises questions about how that work will continue, alongside the immediate challenge of restoring homes and services.

For one 27-year-old woman from Rshaf in the Bint Jbeil district—who requested anonymity for safety reasons—the destruction is visible only from a distance. She was in Spain when someone sent her a satellite image showing her family home reduced to rubble.

"I don’t even know if the cemetery is still there,” she says. “We have no way to access it, and with satellite imagery I can’t tell, because everything is rubble and it’s very pixelated.”

The loss will outlast any ceasefire. Ardiel, who has lived on a UNIFIL base since March, has watched olive trees “hundreds or even thousands of years old” be destroyed. “There’s a legacy here that’s being wiped out,” she said. “Even if the conflict were to end today, the recovery process is going to be intense.”

Yet the desire to return persists. Displaced families repeatedly tell Kaiss: “We don’t need anything but for them to allow us to return. We’ll pitch tents on the rubble of our homes, and we’ll live there.” That’s something Silvin has seen in the most damaged villages already, families “restarting their lives on the rubble.”

“I don’t believe this land will ever be ours again,” said the woman from Rshaf, but she added that if her family could return to their land, they would rebuild. “It’s not even a question.”

This story was originally published on WIRED Middle East.
